extracted.intended_audience: general literate public; writers/readers of moral/satirical essays
extracted.subtask_description: Producing short moral/satirical essays that analyze social habits, vices, and human follies using anecdotes, examples, and ironic commentary. Emphasis is on moral observation, social realism, and disciplined authorial voice rather than technical instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of weather as a meaningful subject
rubrics_metrics.description: “The weather is a nobler and more interesting subject; it is the present state of the skies, and of the earth, on which plenty and famine are suspended, on which millions depend for the necessaries of life.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose subjects that have tangible stakes and observable effects (e.g., weather) rather than trivial gossip; use such concrete subjects to connect moral or social commentary to real consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid attributing human dispositions to the weather or seasons
rubrics_metrics.description: “Our dispositions too frequently change with the colour of the sky... To call upon the sun for peace and gaiety, or deprecate the clouds lest sorrow should overwhelm us, is the cowardice of idleness, and the idolatry of folly.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject facile explanations (e.g., 'creative seasons', 'inspiration only in spring') — in characterization and argument, avoid letting external phenomena become excuses for lack of discipline or virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advocate constancy and discipline over waiting for inspiration
rubrics_metrics.description: “To temperance every day is bright, and every hour is propitious to diligence... He that shall resolutely excite his faculties, or exert his virtues, will soon make himself superior to the seasons.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promote steady, habitual work (temperance, persistence) as the means to intellectual or artistic output; portray productivity as the result of resolved effort rather than occasional illumination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer authentic, deserved fame and particular praise to generic panegyrics
rubrics_metrics.description: “A name... is the free gift of mankind, which must be deserved before it will be granted... Mr. Settle... had a standing elegy and epithalamium... the intermediate pages were, by general terms, left applicable alike to every character.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satirize or avoid formulaic, bought, or generic praise; in praise and characterization be specific—generic encomia reveal vanity and inauthenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expose the vanity of social notices and ceremonial publicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion of marriage announcements and public praise: public declarations of 'eminence', 'beauty', and accomplishment often serve vanity more than truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When depicting society, show how public notices (marriage announcements, portraits of eminence) often conceal mediocrity or serve social posturing; use such contrasts for ironic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustrate consequences of misplaced priorities (ornamental skill vs substantive education)
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative about a wife who forces daughters into needlework so they grow up 'in total ignorance'—Molly asks whether Ireland was in France; Dolly cannot read a chapter in the Bible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When critiquing social practices, show concrete consequences (ignorance, limited prospects) of prioritizing decorative accomplishments over literacy, numeracy, and substantive learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value and defend personal time; portray time-wasting as moral and practical injury
rubrics_metrics.description: “Time once passed never returns... Time therefore ought, above all other kinds of property, to be free from invasion... whoever pays a visit that is not desired, or talks longer than the hearer is willing to attend, is guilty of an injury...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat time as a scarce moral resource. In argument or character portrayal, condemn undue solicitation, idle attendance, and trivial social encroachments that steal time; respect reader/time by avoiding unnecessary padding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirize pretension: show the difference between appearance and real motive
rubrics_metrics.description: Passages on assemblies where attendees' pleasures derive from fashion, rank, or appearing to be pleased rather than true appreciation of the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reveal characters' true motives (vanity, imitation, status-seeking) behind public behavior rather than accepting surface appearances; use juxtaposition and irony to show counterfeit pleasures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use concrete anecdotes and character sketches to ground abstract moral points
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent anecdotes (Mr. Buckram and Miss Dolly Juniper; Mr. Settle's standing elegy; Ned Drugget's country lodging) are used to exemplify general claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support abstract claims with vivid, concise stories of particular people; concrete examples make moral critique persuasive and memorable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condemn gratuitous cruelty in the name of 'research' and avoid sensationalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Strong critique of anatomical novices who 'tear out the living bowels of an animal' and conduct 'living dissections' for ostentation rather than knowledge: 'he surely buys knowledge dear, who learns... at the expense of his humanity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When dealing with scientific or violent detail, evaluate the ethics and utility of the depiction; avoid gratuitous or sensational cruelty that desensitizes readers and undermines moral argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be skeptical of superficial repetition as discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of those who repeat simple experiments (mixing colourless liquors, repeating electrical tinkering) and fancy novelty: 'they mingle them, and produce the effect expected, say it is strange, and mingle them again.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray pseudo-expertise and idle repetition as folly; avoid mistaking reiteration of trivial experiments for genuine insight—use such examples to satirize misplaced scientific pride.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expose small hypocrisies through contrast and cumulative detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Johnson accumulates small ironic details (e.g., needlework rooms, unhelpful wives, shopkeepers aspiring to countryside leisure yet lingering at the shop window) to reveal character contradictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a chain of modest, specific details to build an ironic portrait that exposes hypocrisy or self-deception rather than relying on blunt denunciation.
